source: Heath, Manolopoulou, Baio (2015) A review of methods for the analysis of the expected value of information
finding: Partial EVPI (EVPPI, the value of learning a subset of inputs) is the usable form of VOI. The textbook nested Monte Carlo method is exact in theory but too slow. Regression shortcuts give similar answers in seconds.
numbers: Case study single-parameter EVPPI: two-step Monte Carlo about 55 minutes; GAM regression negligible time; Gaussian process regression 2-4 seconds. Five methods gave broadly similar single-parameter estimates. Authors say report EVPPI to only 1-2 decimals.
limits: One worked case study (treatment model); regression accuracy depends on how smooth net benefit is in the parameters.
agent_relevance: Computing the value of a test must be cheap relative to the test. Prefer a cheap surrogate (regression, EIG over a small sampled hypothesis set) over a nested simulation.

source: Heath, Manolopoulou, Baio (2015) A review of methods for the analysis of the expected value of information
finding: The shortcut methods break down as the parameter set grows. GAM becomes unstable for larger subsets; GP regression cost grows with the cube of the sample size.
numbers: GP cost proportional to N^3 for PSA sample size N. GAM called mathematically unstable for larger subsets (threshold symbol garbled in the extracted text).
limits: Software advice (R, BCEA), not a head-to-head accuracy trial across many models.
agent_relevance: VOI scoring over many uncertain factors at once is the expensive case. Keep S4 test scoring to a few named uncertainties.

source: Heath, Manolopoulou, Baio (2015) A review of methods for the analysis of the expected value of information
finding: Interpretation is a main barrier to using VOI, along with compute. VOI numbers are unbounded in scale, so they only mean something against a cost or threshold.
numbers: Authors list two barriers: interpretation and computational cost.
quote: places an upper bound on the cost of additional research
limits: Review statement, not measured.
agent_relevance: A raw EVPI number has no meaning alone. The agent needs a cost in the same units (tokens, time) before it can say a test is worth running.

source: Thorn, Coast, Andronis (2016) Interpretation of the Expected Value of Perfect Information and Research Recommendations: systematic review and empirical investigation. Medical Decision Making 36(3)
finding: Across applied health EVPI studies, EVPI above research cost is necessary but not sufficient for recommending more research. EVPI was a key driver of recommendations.
numbers: 86 articles included: 66 recommended further research, 13 recommended none, 7 gave no recommendation. Logistic regression on funder, location, disease, year, outcome: none significant.
limits: Abstract only read (Europe PMC). Authors' written recommendations are a proxy for real decisions. Only 13 negative recommendations.
agent_relevance: Even in the field that invented applied EVPI, the bound is a gate and not the decision. Our S4 rule: skip a test whose bound is below its cost, but do not run a test just because the bound exceeds cost.

source: Thorn et al. (2016) same paper, threshold finding
finding: A rough EVPI threshold below which authors did not recommend research was found.
numbers: Threshold about 1.48 million (currency symbol garbled in the source text, likely pounds).
limits: Abstract only. Threshold is an empirical habit of authors, not a theoretical result; depends on population size and willingness to pay.
agent_relevance: Thresholds are context bound. Calibrate the agent's go/no-go cutoff on its own logged test results, not on a borrowed number.

source: Tuffaha, Gordon, Scuffham (2014) Value of information analysis in healthcare: a review of principles and applications. J Med Econ
finding: VOI methods were applied to guide decisions, design studies and set research priorities, but uptake remained limited because of technical and policy barriers.
numbers: No sample counts in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Practice lags theory. Expect that simple, cheap VOI rules get used and heavy ones do not.

source: Brennan, Kharroubi, O'Hagan, Chilcott (2007) Calculating partial expected value of perfect information via Monte Carlo sampling algorithms. Med Decis Making
finding: Naive Monte Carlo EVPI/EVPPI is biased upward at small samples because it takes a maximum over noisy estimates. Shortcut algorithms are inaccurate when inputs are correlated or net benefit is nonlinear.
numbers: Three case studies showed upward bias, shortcut error with correlation, and error with nonlinearity. Suggested: fewer outer samples, more inner samples.
quote: Maxima of Monte Carlo estimates of expectations are biased upward
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Small-sample EIG or EVPI estimates from a few LLM samples will overstate the value of a test (winner's curse). Use enough samples or shrink the estimate.

source: Nelson (2005) Finding useful questions: on Bayesian diagnosticity, probability, impact, and information gain. Psychological Review
finding: Earlier human data could not tell apart five rival value-of-question measures. Computer search found cases where information gain, probability gain and impact strongly disagree with Bayesian diagnosticity, and a new experiment contradicted diagnosticity.
numbers: Five norms compared: diagnosticity, information gain, KL distance, probability gain, impact. Number of subjects not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Rival-theory result: diagnosticity is the loser, the other four were not separated here.
agent_relevance: Do not score tests by likelihood-ratio diagnosticity alone. Use expected information gain or expected error reduction. See also the parallel subfield on diagnosticity of evidence.

source: Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell, Sejnowski (2010) Experience matters: information acquisition optimizes probability gain. Psychological Science
finding: Three experiments, with queries picked by computer to separate the theories, found that probability gain (expected error reduction) explained human search best, ahead of information gain, KL distance, impact and the probability-of-certainty heuristic. Experience-based learning of probabilities gave different behaviour than verbal summary statistics.
numbers: Three experiments; probability gain preference robust in Experiment 3. Subject counts not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Small query-selection tasks with simple binary features; the goal was classification accuracy, which favours probability gain by design.
agent_relevance: The right value measure depends on the goal. If the goal is to pick the final answer correctly, expected accuracy gain is the matching measure; entropy gain fits goals about learning the whole state.

source: Wu, Meder, Filimon, Nelson (2017) Asking better questions: how presentation formats influence information search. JEP:LMC
finding: Format of the numbers changed how well people chose the more useful query. Posterior-probability versions of icon arrays and bar graphs were best and clearly beat the standard probability format.
numbers: Four experiments, N = 2,858, 14 formats, choose between 2 queries to maximise classification accuracy. Accuracy of probability judgments did not predict search performance.
limits: Abstract only. Mixed environments with certain outcomes were hard in every format. Authors propose a take-the-difference heuristic.
agent_relevance: People choose tests by simple heuristics, not by computing posteriors. The way test options are presented (posteriors, counts) will change selection, so present them in code-computed form.

source: Meder, Nelson et al. (2018) Towards a theory of heuristic and optimal planning for sequential information search
finding: Greedy one-step information value is not optimal for sequences of tests. In the Person Game (a 20-questions task) and a two-category task, neither the optimal-experimental-design measures nor the heuristics were optimal over a sequence. Simple heuristics can exactly pick the top single query in some cases.
numbers: Shown by examples and computer simulation; no human sample.
limits: Abstract only. Theory and simulation; the call for human experiments is still open.
agent_relevance: The one-step EVPI/EIG rule (myopic value of information) can fail for multi-test plans. S4 should allow a lookahead of two tests only when tests are cheap to simulate.

source: Bastardi, Shafir (1998) On the pursuit and misuse of useless information. J Pers Soc Psychol
finding: People seek non-instrumental information, meaning information that would not change the choice, and then let it change the choice.
numbers: Abstract gives no figures; several social, consumer and strategic scenarios.
limits: Abstract only. Human data; the failure direction is paying for information with zero decision value.
agent_relevance: The core guardrail case: a test whose result cannot flip the decision has zero value and should be skipped. Add a check: would any possible outcome change the chosen action?

source: Golman, Hagmann, Loewenstein (2017) Information avoidance. Journal of Economic Literature 55(1)
finding: People sometimes avoid information that is useful and free, because information enters utility directly. This breaks the rule that information never has negative value.
numbers: Review, no pooled effect size in abstract.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Applies to emotional stakes (health, finances); an LLM agent has no such stakes.
agent_relevance: Humans are the wrong model for when to stop gathering. The two human errors are over-seeking useless information and avoiding useful information. The agent can fix both by rule.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Choosing the next question by expected entropy reduction, looked ahead over a small tree, beat direct prompting on 20 Questions, simplified medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average success rate improvement 38.1% over direct prompting across LLMs. GPT-4 troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%. GPT-4 closed-set DX diagnosis 97.0%. Llama3-70B closed-set DX 83.7 to 90.4. Five datasets; 20Q up to 20 turns; medical and troubleshooting 5 turns.
limits: The answerer is GPT-4 playing patient/answerer, checked on 10% of interactions. Simplified diagnosis: an answer like no fever does not fully eliminate a disease. Closed-set versions help most.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4: explicit information-gain choice of the next test beats letting the model pick.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Ablation: the uncertainty-based reward is the working part, and gains persist at matched token cost.
numbers: Matched cost (about 9k GPT-4 tokens): Adapted-ToT depth 4 vs UoT depth 3 on 20Q 40.9 vs 54.4, medical 86.7 vs 92.5, troubleshooting 63.7 vs 66.0. Adding the uncertainty reward to plain ToT adds 5.9% on average; swapping UoT's reward for a self-evaluation reward lowers success.
limits: Gains are largest on 20Q and smallest on troubleshooting. Pruned UoT used about 4.7k tokens and got 48.1 / 88.4 / 63.2.
agent_relevance: Self-rated usefulness of a test is the weak signal. A computed reward for the test (probability mass split) is the strong one. Matches G5: code selects.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Choosing questions by estimated expected information gain from the LLM's own predictive distributions, with a filtered hypothesis set, roughly doubled success in 20 Questions versus asking the model for a question.
numbers: On average +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting. 100 targets per set (Animals, Celebrities, Things). GPT-4o Animals 45 to 93; Mistral-Large Celebrities 19 to 91; Llama-3.1-8B Things 10 to 26; Qwen2.5-72B Celebrities 32 to 84. Never decreased in any setup.
limits: 20 Questions with yes/no/maybe answerer and unrestricted target space. Authors say their Prompt-Only baseline is stronger than in earlier work, so gains are against a fair baseline. Success is final guess exact match.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent measurement that an explicit EIG step beats prompting across six LLMs. Needs a hypothesis set generated and filtered by code.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Ablation shows how EIG is computed matters. Predictive entropy alone, a data-estimation shortcut and implicit-max variants all fall below full EIG with filtering and belief updates.
numbers: GPT-4o Celebrities: BED-LLM 86, Entropy-only 64, Split 63, CoT 63, Prompt-Only 45 (Entropy, Data-Estimation and Impl. Max columns read from a garbled table). Standard errors about 3-5 points on 100 items per cell.
limits: Entropy-only is close to full EIG on easy sets (Animals GPT-4o 88 vs 93) and far on harder ones. The Split baseline (deterministic split of hypotheses) is a strong, cheap rival: Animals GPT-4o 83.
agent_relevance: A cheap split-the-hypotheses rule recovers much of the gain. Use it first, then full EIG only where hypothesis sets are hard.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Scoring candidate clarifying questions by information gain over self-sampled candidate solutions raised code accuracy after four questions, most for weaker models.
numbers: HumanEval, 48 non-trivial tasks. GPT-3.5 after 4 questions: binary base 70.8 vs EIG 85.6; open base 75.9 vs 85.0. Llama3-8B open: 64.8 vs 75.5. GPT-4o-mini binary 79.6 vs 81.5; open 83.5 vs 83.8.
limits: Gap shrinks for more capable models and is near zero for GPT-4o-mini open questions. At turn 1 GPT-4o-mini binary EIG (73.6) was below base (74.6). Test answers simulated by hidden test cases; APPS has lower accuracy but same ordering.
agent_relevance: VOI helps most where the base model is weak at choosing tests. If our agent's base model is strong, expect smaller returns; test on our own logs before paying for the machinery.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Boundary condition: in 20 Questions, EIG weighted by the LLM's own log-probabilities did worse than plain prompting in some models; uniform-weighted EIG was best.
numbers: Score after 10 questions. GPT-3.5: EIG-uniform 6.2, EIG-logprobs 4.1, implicit-ToT 5.1, implicit 4.9. Llama3-70B: uniform 6.3, logprobs 3.9, implicit 5.9. GPT-4o-mini: uniform 6.8, logprobs 6.0, implicit 5.5. 15 animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds.
limits: Reading assumes higher score is better (the paper says EIG-uniform outperforms by a significant margin). Later work (BED-LLM) says this paper's EIG implementation was weaker than theirs.
agent_relevance: LLM-assigned probabilities are miscalibrated; they can make EIG worse than not using it. Use counts over samples, not model-stated probabilities.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Models are good at the arithmetic of a problem but poor at spotting which single missing fact to ask for in logic and planning tasks.
numbers: GSM-Q and GSME-Q above 80% accuracy for strong models. Logic-Q and Planning-Q under 50% for all tested models: o1-preview Logic-Q about 49.9%, Planning-Q about 42.3% (zero-shot CoT row of a garbled table); GPT-4o Logic-Q about 30%. Models include Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemma 2.
limits: Multiple choice question selection, exactly one missing variable. Accuracy falls with more variables, constraints and search depth (Spearman about -0.1 to -0.4, some -0.5, in Logic-Q and Planning-Q).
agent_relevance: Asking is a distinct skill. A model that solves the full problem still cannot reliably say what to ask. Use code (backward search over a constraint model) to name the missing fact where possible.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Control: restricting to problems the model solved when fully specified did not fix question choice.
numbers: Logic-Q accuracy changed by 0.0 to 1.1 points after filtering; Planning-Q rose by about 4-19 points; GSM variants moved from -10 to +39 points. Neither Logic-Q nor Planning-Q reached 100%.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Filtering keeps examples where at least one well-specified variant was solved.
agent_relevance: Rules out the simple explanation that failures are only reasoning failures. Supports a separate programmatic step for identifying what to test.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: question-asking LLMs and a benchmark for reliable interactive clinical reasoning
finding: Letting models ask whenever they like made diagnosis worse. A confidence gate for when to ask recovered the loss and more.
numbers: Directly prompted questioning cut accuracy 11.3% relative versus the same starting information with no questions. Best gate (1-5 confidence scale, rationale, self-consistency factor 3) improved on BASIC by 22.3% and on non-interactive Initial by 12.1%, but stayed 10.3% below the full-information upper bound. GPT-4 iMEDQA: Full 79.7, Initial 54.5, BASIC 55.4, best 66.1.
quote: directly prompting state-of-the-art LLMs to ask questions degrades performance
limits: Patient simulated by an LLM from atomic facts. Self-consistency alone hurt unless paired with rationale generation. Multiple-choice medical QA.
agent_relevance: Asking is not free value. Without a when-to-ask test, questions add noise. Real-data demonstration that EVPI-style gating (ask only if the answer could change the decision) matters.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions: enhancing LLMs with preference optimization and expected information gain
finding: Training Llama-2-7B on pairs of high-EIG versus low-EIG questions (DPO) raised question informativeness and game success, with partial transfer to other domains.
numbers: INLG 20 Questions: zero-shot success 56.7%, EIG 0.34; fine-tuning 46.6%, 0.41; DPO 68.9%, 0.45. Things: 51.1 to 61.1%; Celebrities 71.1 to 72.2%. Larger candidate sets: BigBench success 17.2 to 31.0% but EIG 0.31 to 0.28.
limits: Small test sets (8-item candidate sets in main table). Plain fine-tuning raised EIG yet lowered success, so higher EIG alone did not guarantee wins.
agent_relevance: Higher EIG per question is not the same as winning. Track outcome flips, not only the information score.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships: asking questions in Battleship with language-informed program sampling (CogSci 2024)
finding: Sampling a few questions from an LLM and keeping the one with highest computed EIG matched average human informativeness. LLMs alone asked low-information questions and the vision model gave no gain.
numbers: Human data: N = 40 participants, 18 boards, 605 question-board pairs; mean human EIG 1.27 bits, best human 3.61, 97% of human questions informative (EIG > 0). Single LLM samples averaged EIG about 0.65-0.66 (GPT-4, CodeLlama); grammar prior 0.36. With k = 5 samples both LLMs approached the human mean but fell short of the top 10-20% of human questions. GPT-4V gave no improvement over text.
limits: Single closed game with a computable hypothesis space. Only a few models.
agent_relevance: Best-of-k questions scored by code is cheap and works (k = 5 in this task). It does not reach expert-level questions.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational metareasoning for large language models
finding: Training with a reward that charges for reasoning tokens (value of computation) cut tokens with no loss in accuracy and made reasoning length track difficulty.
numbers: 23-45% fewer tokens across three models versus few-shot CoT and STaR; 35-42% fewer than few-shot prompting and 23-32% fewer than STaR; out-of-distribution on MMLU-CF 28-36% fewer than STaR; up to 50.3% shorter on easy items for Llama-3.2-3B. Trained on 4,096 samples from four datasets.
limits: Requires training (expert iteration) on Llama-3.2-3B and 3.1-8B scale models; not a prompt-only result. Reductions smaller for physics and engineering.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot train, but the finding says value-of-computation is learnable and that effort should scale with difficulty. A programmatic stand-in is to stop when checks pass.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stopping the sampling when the vote lead is statistically stable saves most samples. This treats each extra sample as a test whose value falls as agreement grows.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: up to 7.9x fewer samples with average accuracy drop under 0.1%; average 3.3x fewer. GPT-3.5 4.4x fewer with under 0.2% drop; Vicuna-13B 1.9x fewer.
limits: Assumes samples are exchangeable draws; this is not true of one model's correlated errors (guardrail G4), so the stop can be confidently wrong.
agent_relevance: A working stop rule for sampling. Pair it with a held-out check so agreement is not read as proof.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape sky-high cost: early-stopping self-consistency (ESC)
finding: Sampling in small windows and stopping when a window agrees cut samples sharply with similar accuracy.
numbers: Average samples reduced: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%.
limits: Same exchangeability caveat. Coin Flip with GPT-4 is already 100% accurate, so savings there are easy.
agent_relevance: Independent replication of the Adaptive-Consistency idea: the value of one more sample drops fast once agreement appears on tasks the model usually gets right.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly across turns, which undermines any value-of-information calculation that depends on their stated probabilities. Fine-tuning on a Bayesian model's predictions fixed it better than fine-tuning on correct answers.
numbers: Flight recommendation task, 5 rounds, 624 simulated users, 100 new option sets per round. Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1, Gemini 1.5: little improvement after round 1 and far below the Bayesian assistant. 48 users also answered by humans, who improved more than most LLMs but still fell short of the Bayesian assistant. CoT and numeric prompts gave no meaningful gain. Exact accuracy figures are in figures, not in text.
limits: Exact accuracy numbers not recoverable from text extraction. Tuned only the 7-9B models.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a model-stated posterior as the input to EVPI. Keep probability bookkeeping in code.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Models did not explore well on bandits unless history was summarised outside the model.
numbers: Only one configuration succeeded: GPT-4 with chain of thought plus an externally summarised history of sufficient statistics. GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 across many prompts failed.
quote: the models do not robustly engage in exploration without substantial interventions
limits: Simple multi-armed bandits, not open-ended search.
agent_relevance: The agent should keep the statistics (counts, outcomes of tests) in code and show the model a summary. Raw history in the prompt does not give sound exploration.

source: Andukuri, Franken, Gerstenberg, Goodman (2024) STaR-GATE: teaching language models to ask clarifying questions
finding: Self-training a model on questions that raise the probability of a gold response raised win rate of final answers.
numbers: 25,500 persona-task prompts; after two iterations responses preferred over the initial model on 72% of tasks.
limits: Simulated roleplayer with fixed latent preferences; win rate judged against a gold response from an oracle.
agent_relevance: Gives a learnable reward for a question: how much it raises the chance of the good answer. A logged flip rate per test can play the same role.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting human preferences with language models (GATE)
finding: With real people, LM-led elicitation was often more informative than user-written prompts or labelled examples and was less mentally demanding.
numbers: Three domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning), preregistered. GATE beat no elicitation in all domains (p < .05 except email, where only generative active learning was significant); improved over user-written prompts in 6 of 10 settings (absolute) and 7 of 10 (AUC). Generative yes/no questions beat user prompts in every setting.
limits: Significance against baselines only established in content recommendation and email; moral reasoning underpowered. Effect sizes are in figures, not in the text.
agent_relevance: Human-in-the-loop evidence that model-chosen questions can add information; the benefit is conditional on real variation in answers.

source: Zhang, Knox, Choi (2025) Modeling future conversation turns to teach LLMs to ask clarifying questions (ICLR 2025)
finding: Labelling preferences by simulating what happens in future turns (the outcome value of a clarifying question) beat labelling on the prior context alone.
numbers: About 5% F1 improvement against the answer set over three base LLMs; 3% better accuracy deciding when to ask versus answer directly. About 56% of NQ-Open queries identified as ambiguous in their pipeline.
limits: Open-domain QA with simulated users; small absolute gains.
agent_relevance: Supports valuing a question by its downstream outcome, not by how good it looks. A simulate-the-answer step before choosing a test fits S4.

source: Wang, Zollo, Zemel, Namkoong (2025) Adaptive elicitation of latent information using natural language
finding: A meta-learned LM that simulates future answers to estimate how much a new question reduces uncertainty outperformed baselines on 20 Questions, opinion polling and adaptive student assessment.
numbers: No figures read; abstract level only.
limits: PDF fetched but only the abstract read. Needs meta-training.
agent_relevance: Another route to EIG without a named hypothesis set. Not usable without training.
